name: From Tally Marks to Proof: A Story of Number
description: Babylonian sixties, an Indian zero, Greek proofs, calculus and unsolved riddles: how people built mathematics and who dared to push it further.

checkpoints.name: Counting and shape
checkpoints.note: Babylonians counted in sixties and worked out good values of pi. Greek thinkers added proof: Pythagoras, Euclid's Elements, Archimedes on circles, and the study of prime numbers.

checkpoints.name: Zero and algebra
checkpoints.note: Hypatia taught geometry in Alexandria, Indian scholars such as Aryabhata built a place-value system with nine digits, and Brahmagupta set out rules for zero as a number. Al-Khwarizmi's book on balancing equations gave algebra its name.

checkpoints.name: Logarithms, chance and calculus
checkpoints.note: Logarithms and the slide rule eased heavy sums, Descartes joined algebra to geometry, and Fermat and others began probability. Newton and Leibniz then built calculus, the mathematics of change.

checkpoints.name: New worlds of thought
checkpoints.note: Mathematicians imagined curved, non-Euclidean spaces, turned logic into algebra with Boole, and tamed infinity with set theory. Riemann's hypothesis and the four colour problem posed new puzzles.

checkpoints.name: Proof and its limits
checkpoints.note: Noether and Ramanujan showed new depths. Godel proved that some truths cannot be proved, Turing turned calculation into computing, and Wiles, Perelman and Mirzakhani tackled long-standing problems.
